evidence.claim: Highway 21 crosses the Boston Mountains for 35 miles between Highway 64 and the Buffalo National River.
evidence.quote: For 35 miles, Highway 21 from Highway 64 to the Buffalo National River traverses the Boston Mountains region of the Ozark Mountains.

evidence.claim: The Ozark Highlands Scenic Byway follows ridges between stream headwaters through rugged terrain.
evidence.quote: Traversing ridges between headwaters of major streams with panoramic views, colorful flora, and rugged terrain

evidence.claim: The Arkansas Department of Transportation presents the byway as a forest drive with recreational opportunities and views before the river.
evidence.quote: The Byway, designated in 2005, offers a serene drive through the Ozark National Forest as well as many recreational opportunities and striking vistas before arriving at the nation’s first National River.

evidence.claim: The road through this corridor has two lanes. Across the Boston Mountains, forested uplands stand above deeply eroded valleys, with sandstone and shale capping the highest ridges.
evidence.quote: The route is a two-lane highway with the exception of a brief concurrency with US 62, a four-lane highway, in Berryville.

evidence.claim: Across the Boston Mountains, forested uplands stand above deeply eroded valleys, with sandstone and shale capping the highest ridges.
evidence.quote: The highest ridges and peaks are capped by Pennsylvanian sandstone and shale. The deeply eroded valleys are cut into Mississippian limestones

evidence.claim: forested uplands
evidence.quote: northern red oak, southern red oak, white oak, and hickories usually dominate the uplands

evidence.claim: In 2005, the Arkansas State Highway and Transportation Department designated this portion of Highway 21 as the Ozark Highlands Scenic Byway.
evidence.quote: A portion of Highway 21 was designated as the Ozark Highlands Scenic Byway in 2005 by the Arkansas State Highway and Transportation Department (AHTD).

evidence.claim: The scenic corridor occupies part of a longer highway, which continues north across US 62 to the Missouri state line.
evidence.quote: The route runs 99.14 miles (159.55 km) from U.S. Route 64 (US 64) in Clarksville north across US 62 to the Missouri state line.

evidence.claim: Highway 21 also serves as a major route to the Ozark National Forest and Ozark Highlands Trail.
evidence.quote: The highway is popular as a major route to the Ozark National Forest, the Ozark Highlands Trail

evidence.claim: Start at US 64 in Clarksville and travel north toward the Ozark National Forest.
evidence.quote: The route begins at US 64 in Clarksville near the Clarksville Municipal Airport and runs north to the Ozark National Forest.

evidence.claim: Ozone lies on Highway 21, 11.5 miles north of Clarksville.
evidence.quote: Ozone is located on Arkansas Highway 21, 11.5 miles (18.5 km) north of Clarksville.

evidence.claim: Farther along, Highway 21 shares Highway 16 before turning north at Edwards Junction toward Boxley.
evidence.quote: The route begins a concurrency with Highway 16 until Edwards Junction when Highway 21 turns north and serves as a southern terminus for Highway 43 at Boxley.

evidence.claim: The byway ends near Boxley at the Buffalo National River.
evidence.quote: runs north to the Buffalo National River near Boxley.

evidence.claim: Boxley Bridge carries Highway 21 across the upper river.
evidence.quote: Boxley Bridge – located on the upper end of the river along Arkansas Highway 21.

evidence.claim: Ozone’s school gives this Highway 21 community a distinctive piece of public architecture.
evidence.quote: The Ozone School is a historic school building at 14137 Arkansas Highway 21 in Ozone, Arkansas.

evidence.claim: Built in 1942 with Works Progress Administration funding, it served as a public school until 1957, when the district consolidated with Lamar.
evidence.quote: The school was built in 1942 with funding from the Works Progress Administration, and was used as a public school until 1957, when the local district was consolidated with that of Lamar.

evidence.claim: Fieldstone blocks form its single story. A projecting entrance tower has arched openings below a crosswise gabled roof, while exposed rafter ends mark the main roof.
evidence.quote: It is a single-story masonry structure, built out of coursed fieldstone blocks and covered by gable-on-hip roof with exposed rafter ends.  Its front entrance is sheltered by a distinctive projecting tower, with arched openings at the base and a transverse gabled roof above.

evidence.claim: The building entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.
evidence.quote: The building was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 2015.

evidence.claim: The Mulberry River is a 70-mile tributary of the Arkansas River.
evidence.quote: The Mulberry River is a 70-mile-long (110 km) tributary of the Arkansas River

evidence.claim: It rises in southwestern Newton County, travels west through Johnson and Franklin counties, then turns south into the Arkansas River valley.
evidence.quote: It rises in southwestern Newton County and initially flows generally westwardly through Johnson and Franklin counties.  In Franklin County it turns southward into the valley of the Arkansas River

evidence.claim: Most of its course lies in the Ozark National Forest.
evidence.quote: The Mulberry River flows for most of its length through the Ozark National Forest in the Ozarks.

evidence.claim: In 1992, the federal government protected its uppermost 56 miles through the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System.
evidence.quote: The uppermost 56 miles of the Mulberry River were designated for protection as part of the National Wild and Scenic Rivers System by the United States government in 1992.

evidence.claim: Its character changes with the water level: high water can make paddling hazardous, while at low water the river barely flows. Season and recent rainfall strongly influence the flow.
evidence.quote: The river varies greatly in its flow depending upon the season and recent precipitation

evidence.claim: high water can make paddling hazardous, while at low water the river barely flows.
evidence.quote: paddling can be hazardous if the water level is high. At low water the river is placid and barely flows.

evidence.claim: At Boxley Bridge, Highway 21 reaches the upper Buffalo River.
evidence.quote: Boxley Bridge – located on the upper end of the river along Arkansas Highway 21.

evidence.claim: The river flows north through Boxley to Ponca before turning east across northern Arkansas.
evidence.quote: The river flows north through Boxley to Ponca, where it then begins an eastward trek across northern Arkansas

evidence.claim: Along the upper river, steep gradients and fast water give way downstream to a flatter, slower course.
evidence.quote: Along the upper river, the gradient is steep and the water is fast, leveling and slowing as the river runs its course.

evidence.claim: Congress established the Buffalo National River on March 1, 1972, ending recurring Army Corps of Engineers plans to dam the river.
evidence.quote: The Buffalo National River was established by an Act of Congress on March 1, 1972, ending the recurring plans of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to construct one or more dams on the river.

evidence.claim: It was the first National River designated in the United States.
evidence.quote: was the first National River to be designated in the United States.

evidence.claim: The Arkansas Department of Transportation singles out the area near the river as a place to watch for elk.
evidence.quote: Watch for elk near the Buffalo National River
